analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, bond, and derivatives trades to fund public programs, with the tax refunded for most lower- and middle-income households.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place a small tax on each purchase of stocks (0.5% of the trade's value), bonds (0.1%), and derivatives (0.005%). Exchanges and brokers would collect it. Low-income and moderate-income households — those making under $50,000 a year, or $75,000 for couples — would get every dollar of the tax they pay refunded, so the cost would land mainly on big traders and wealthy investors. The money raised would go to the government to spend on families, infrastructure, the environment, and financial security. The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning under $50,000 a year ($75,000 for couples) would pay effectively nothing, because the bill refunds any tax they personally incur on their own investments. Beyond that, the federal government gains a new revenue stream from high-volume securities trading — which could fund programs for families, infrastructure, and the environment, as the bill's title states — and, if the tax discourages rapid speculation as supporters intend, long-term investors benefit from a somewhat more stable market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income households and public programs

how_it_helps.text: It raises revenue from high-volume securities trading — 0.5% on stock purchases, 0.1% on bond purchases, 0.005% on derivatives — that the bill's title says would be invested in families, communities, infrastructure, and the environment.

It refunds every dollar of the tax paid by households with modified adjusted gross income under $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers), so most lower- and middle-income people would pay nothing out of pocket.
By adding a small cost to each trade, it is designed to discourage rapid, high-frequency speculation and reduce market volatility.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on whoever buys and sells securities most: high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, and large institutional investors. The tax applies to every purchase, so some cost would also be passed through mutual funds and retirement accounts to ordinary investors — but the bill refunds the tax entirely for households under the income limits, leaving the burden mainly on wealthier investors and high-volume traders above them.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every purchase of stocks, bonds, and other securities, not just rapid speculation, so the cost would be partly passed on to ordinary investors through the funds and retirement accounts they hold, and the offsetting credit disappears above $50,000 of income ($75,000 for joint filers), leaving middle-income savers to bear it.

The tax is collected on each transaction, including the net payments on derivatives, and stacking of small levies across frequent trades can raise costs in ways that reduce market liquidity and increase the cost of capital — a well-documented risk with transaction taxes of this type.

Because the tax reaches purchases by U.S. persons even when they occur abroad, trading may migrate to foreign venues or new instruments, which past transaction-tax experience suggests can produce less revenue than projected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for most households is indirect: revenue for public programs, a modest rebate for lower-income savers, and, if the tax curbs high-frequency speculation as supporters claim, a slightly more stable market. The costs are real and fall partly on ordinary people: every purchase of a stock or bond is taxed, and savers above the $50,000/$75,000 credit phase-out — much of the middle class with retirement accounts — would bear it with no offset. Critics also point to the experience of transaction taxes abroad, where trading moved offshore and revenue came in below projections. A narrow tax aimed at high-frequency and speculative trades would have targeted the stated problem more precisely; taxing every trade, including routine index-fund purchases, is broad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Barbara Lee introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee took no further action: the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms and other high-volume traders avoided the new tax, and no revenue was raised for the programs the bill was written to fund.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Wall Street trading firms and high-frequency traders
industries.note: A tax on every stock, bond, and derivatives transaction hits high-volume trading firms hardest, since they make the most trades; the bill also directs regulators to write rules to prevent trading from being routed around the tax through foreign or non-U.S. structures. For ordinary people, the tax's purpose is to fund public programs and curb speculative volatility.

Funds and 401(k)-style accounts buy securities constantly and would absorb or pass on the tax, raising costs for savers — but households under $50,000/$75,000 of income get a full rebate, and slower, more stable markets can benefit long-term investors.

industries.industry: Stock exchanges, brokers, and clearing firms
industries.note: Exchanges and brokers are made legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on trades they process, adding compliance work and cost.
